items.title: Xoscar: unauthenticated code execution in the Xinference actor pool
items.summary: Xoscar, the actor framework behind the Xinference model server, runs attacker code from any unauthenticated TCP message sent to its actor pool. VulnCheck published CVE-2026-49950 on October 13 with no fixed version available.

explainer.tagline: Xoscar's actor pool deserializes every inbound TCP message with cloudpickle before it checks the message type, and before any authentication.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-49950 on October 13, 2026, after a 120-day coordinated disclosure deadline passed without a vendor fix. Valentin Lobstein found the flaw in Xorbits Xoscar, the Python actor and RPC framework that the Xinference model server uses to connect supervisors, workers and model pools. VulnCheck is the assigning CNA and rates the flaw 9.3 on CVSS 4.0.
explainer.howItWorks: The actor pool's socket receive path hands raw bytes to cloudpickle.loads() before it checks what kind of message arrived. A Python pickle payload carrying a __reduce__ gadget therefore runs during deserialization. The channel has no authentication, no restricted unpickler and no class allowlist, so the one byte of protocol version read first is framing, not a security control.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Every released version of Xoscar from 0.1.0 through 0.11.2 is affected, including the current release. VulnCheck reports that Xinference binds the actor pool to 0.0.0.0 in distributed mode, which puts the port within reach of an internal network, and that the pool process often runs as root on GPU nodes.
explainer.whatToDo: Block network access to Xoscar actor pool ports at the host and network level, and keep Xinference workers on an isolated segment rather than one reachable from general internal traffic. Reduce the pool process away from root where the deployment allows it, and watch the Xoscar repository for a release above 0.11.2.

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: No fixed version, disclosure deadline passed

faq.q: Am I affected if I run Xinference?
faq.a: Xinference users are exposed when the deployment runs in distributed mode, because VulnCheck reports the Xoscar actor pool binds to 0.0.0.0 by default and accepts unauthenticated messages. Anyone able to reach that TCP port on the internal network can run code in the pool process. Single-process local setups that never open the actor pool port to other hosts are not reachable the same way.

faq.q: Is there a patch for CVE-2026-49950 in Xoscar?
faq.a: No fixed version of Xoscar exists. The flaw affects every release from 0.1.0 through 0.11.2, and 0.11.2 is the current release, published on October 7, 2026. VulnCheck says its 120-day coordinated disclosure deadline passed without a vendor fix, so defenders have to rely on network controls and privilege reduction rather than an upgrade.

faq.q: How do I check whether my Xoscar actor pool is exposed?
faq.a: Defenders should look for Xoscar actor pool ports listening on all interfaces rather than loopback on each Xinference supervisor and worker host, then confirm from another host whether those ports accept connections. VulnCheck notes the pool often runs as root on GPU nodes, so any reachable port deserves treatment as a path to full host compromise.

faq.q: Does authentication on Xinference protect the actor pool?
faq.a: Authentication on the Xinference API does not protect the Xoscar actor pool. VulnCheck describes the actor pool channel as having no authentication of its own, no restricted unpickler and no class allowlist, so any peer that can open the TCP port is trusted. The only check before deserialization is a one-byte protocol version, which VulnCheck calls a framing check rather than a security control.

items.title: Energize Lab Eilik: unauthenticated model admin and leaked child data
items.summary: Energize Lab's Eilik and EilikO desk robots expose unauthenticated AI model administration and leak conversation and child profile data, says an audit by Sammy Azdoufal. Nine CVE ids are reserved and the vendor has not replied.

explainer.tagline: Energize Lab's Eilik robots let anyone on the internet administer the AI model behind them, with nine CVE ids reserved and no vendor reply.
explainer.whatHappened: Sammy Azdoufal, an independent researcher who bought the robot, published an audit of the Energize Lab Eilik and EilikO desk companions on GitHub, dated 2026-10-13. The GitHub Advisory Database listed five EnergizeLab advisories from the audit on 2026-10-15. Energize Lab answered none of the researcher's contact attempts, the disclosure log states, and the audit reports 57 findings.
explainer.howItWorks: Eilik's voice pipeline sends speech to a cloud LLM and plays a synthesized reply back, and the services behind that pipeline check no credentials. Unauthenticated model administration endpoints let a remote caller change model configuration and switch the model in use at runtime, which the write-up says can also swap the synthesized voice and the robot's personality. A file read on the admin panel returns a .env file holding JWT signing secrets, so a caller can forge a super-admin token, and the researcher reports that the nightly profiling pipeline accepts prompt injection and that profile notes in a public Redis key are treated as ground truth the robot will defend.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Owners of the Eilik and EilikO robots and operators of the EnergizeLab AI Station are exposed, because most of the flaws sit in the vendor's cloud services rather than in a setting an owner controls. The AI Station firmware image is separate: it ships default root credentials with SSH enabled, rated 8.8. Conversation transcripts are stored in cleartext and a nightly job extracts child profile fields, the audit says.
explainer.whatToDo: Treat anything said near an Eilik as published, since owners cannot patch the vendor's cloud and the audit reports no secret rotated since discovery. Keep the robot and any AI Station off network segments that carry other sensitive devices, because the firmware accepts default root logins over SSH.

quickFacts.value: Missing authentication and authorization on cloud AI services, plus default firmware credentials

faq.q: Is the Eilik robot flaw fixed?
faq.a: Eight of the Eilik audit's findings were fixed as of the 2026-10-13 retest, leaving 32 of 40 remotely testable findings open, according to the researcher's disclosure log. The log adds that no secret has been rotated since discovery, that the JWT signing secret is unchanged, and that the MySQL and Redis instances stay publicly reachable.

faq.q: Which CVE ids cover the Eilik and EnergizeLab AI Station flaws?
faq.a: Nine CVE ids, CVE-2026-105032 through CVE-2026-105040, are reserved for the audit, and the researcher's mapping file lists the finding behind each one. The GitHub Advisory Database listed five EnergizeLab advisories on 2026-10-15, among them CVE-2026-105038 for unauthenticated model administration at CVSS 9.8 and CVE-2026-105033 for default root credentials on the AI Station at CVSS 8.8.

faq.q: Can an attacker change which model an Eilik robot uses?
faq.a: Unauthenticated model administration endpoints in the Eilik and EilikO inference services let a remote caller change model configuration and switch the model in use at runtime, the GitHub advisory for CVE-2026-105038 states, scoring that 9.8. The researcher's write-up says the same class of endpoint can swap the language model, the synthesized voice and the robot's personality.

faq.q: Did Energize Lab respond to the Eilik disclosure?
faq.a: Energize Lab did not reply through any channel, the disclosure log states, naming email, an SMTP relay, a Feishu bot, an in-app feedback ticket and a press inquiry from The Verge. First contact was attempted in June 2026, the master report was finalized on 2026-09-01, and a 72-hour final deadline communicated on 2026-09-15 expired without an answer.

items.title: CL-UNK-1211: Unit 42 sees LLM traces in Linux espionage tooling
items.summary: Unit 42 reports that an espionage cluster it tracks as CL-UNK-1211 hit government Linux servers from October 2025 to April 2026, and that comments left in the attacker's scripts suggest an LLM wrote or ran them.

explainer.tagline: Unit 42 reports that an espionage cluster it calls CL-UNK-1211 left LLM-style comments in the scripts it ran against government Linux servers.
explainer.whatHappened: Unit 42 published an analysis of CL-UNK-1211 on 2026-10-15, an intrusion cluster that targeted government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure between October 2025 and April 2026. Roey Porat and Tom Fakterman write that several of the attacker's scripts carried conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments, which they read as a sign the code was generated by an LLM or run by an automated AI agent. Unit 42 names no AI product or model on the attacker's side, and has not tied the cluster to a state or to a criminal group.
explainer.howItWorks: Web shells on Linux servers gave the cluster entry, and persistence came from setting auto_prepend_file across PHP configurations in /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/, so a malicious file loads before any other PHP script. A hijacked .bashrc imitated a sudo password prompt and wrote captured passwords to a file named Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, which Unit 42 says was evasion naming and not a SolarWinds compromise. The authors name a custom cross-platform Go remote access trojan, SysGoRAT, which uses WebSocket command and control and renames itself to blend in. Besides the LLM-style comments, Unit 42 cites heavy Base64 command encoding and switching between PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python as traits consistent with AI assistance.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure running Linux servers and databases are the reported targets. Unit 42 publishes no victim count, and lists at least seven command and control servers, 17 IP addresses and four domains. The cluster also used LinPEAS, PwnKit and a custom Go scanner for the React Server Components flaw CVE-2025-55182.
explainer.whatToDo: Enforce strict outbound firewall rules and alert when standard utilities spawn interactive shells. Monitor Linux servers for PHP configuration changes, shell history clearing and log tampering, and check the indicators the report publishes.

items.title: VulnBump: a dependency fix only counts if the tests still pass
items.summary: VulnBump is an open benchmark from Snyk that counts a dependency upgrade as fixed only when the vulnerabilities are gone and the build and tests still pass. Four approaches scored 46.9% to 90.2% across 307 tasks.

explainer.tagline: VulnBump is Snyk's open benchmark that counts a dependency fix only when the vulnerability is gone and the tests still pass.
explainer.whatHappened: Snyk posted VulnBump to arXiv on 2026-10-12 and published the scores in a write-up on 2026-10-15. Gabija Pasiunaite, Ryan McMorrow, Brian Clark, Liran Tal and Luke Tu built 307 dependency upgrade tasks from 43 real repositories, covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities across six package managers. The harness and all 43 evaluation cases are released under Apache 2.0.
explainer.howItWorks: Each VulnBump task runs in a fresh container and passes only when four gates clear: dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and previously passing tests still pass. Every entrant ran on Claude Sonnet 5.5 with a 110-turn limit, so the comparison measures the harness around the model rather than the model itself. The authors report that Claude Code's failures usually leave the vulnerability in place, while the Snyk agent's failures usually break the build or the tests.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Teams that let coding agents raise dependency upgrades are the audience, across Maven, Gradle, npm, Yarn, pip and Poetry. The authors report that 163 of the 307 tasks needed more than a version bump, and that major upgrades and large framework migrations stay hard for every approach tested.
explainer.whatToDo: Check an agent's dependency fix by rescanning, rebuilding and rerunning the previously passing tests, rather than accepting a version bump as done. Weigh the scores against the limits Snyk states: one model, one run per upgrade, Snyk Open Source as the judge, and no penalty for new vulnerabilities an upgrade introduced.

items.title: goose: read-only tool annotations skipped Manual Approval
items.summary: CVE-2026-109561 let prompt-injected calls to tools marked read-only run without a prompt in goose's Manual Approval mode, once a session had used Smart Approval. goose 1.28.0 to 1.43.x are affected, fixed in 1.44.0.

explainer.tagline: goose kept read-only tool annotations from an earlier Smart Approval session, so Manual Approval mode stopped asking before those tools ran.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-109561 on October 12, 2026, an approval bypass in goose, the open source AI agent that the project says is part of the Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation. The advisory credits Akıner Kısa and Project Loupe. The NVD published the record the same day, three months after the goose maintainers shipped the code change.
explainer.howItWorks: Approval decisions rested on tool annotations that outlived the mode which honored them. A session run in Smart Approval mode stored read-only annotations, and update_goose_mode never cleared them, so PermissionInspector::inspect kept treating those tools as already allowed after the user switched to Manual Approval. A prompt-injected call to any tool annotated readOnlyHint: true then ran with no prompt, which VulnCheck classes as incorrect authorization (CWE-863).
explainer.whoIsAffected: Versions 1.28.0 up to 1.44.0 of goose are affected, and only in sessions that used Smart Approval before the user selected Manual Approval. The patched release came out on July 23, 2026, so an installation pinned below 1.44.0 is the condition that still matters.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade goose to 1.44.0 or later, the release VulnCheck lists as fixed. Check version pins in container images, lockfiles and installer scripts, because the fix is old enough that a stale pin is the likely reason for still running an affected build.

quickFacts.label: Weakness
quickFacts.value: CWE-863, annotations not cleared on a mode change

quickFacts.label: Disclosed
quickFacts.value: October 12, 2026 by VulnCheck, same day at the NVD

faq.q: Which goose versions need the CVE-2026-109561 fix?
faq.a: goose 1.28.0 up to 1.44.0 carries the Manual Approval bypass, and 1.44.0 is the fixed release. VulnCheck lists no workaround, so an upgrade is the action. Because that release shipped in July 2026, a current install is already covered, and the versions that still matter are the ones held back by a pin.

faq.q: Why did goose get a CVE for something fixed in July 2026?
faq.a: VulnCheck published the goose advisory on October 12, 2026, while the code change shipped in release 1.44.0 on July 23, 2026, listed there as a bug fix called enforce manual approval for code mode. The public security record arrived about three months after the patch, so a team that tracks goose by CVE meets this flaw only this week.

faq.q: Does Smart Approval mode in goose still use read-only annotations?
faq.a: Yes. Pull request 10528 keeps read-only annotations and cached allows in effect for Smart Approval, and stops them from carrying over into Manual Approval. The same change marks the execute_bash tool in Code Mode as mutating and destructive, so goose no longer treats that tool as safe to allow without asking.

items.title: Junie CLI: an untrusted project's MCP config could run code
items.summary: CVE-2026-111091 let code run in JetBrains Junie CLI through an untrusted project's MCP server configuration. JetBrains published the flaw on October 15 and fixed it in Junie CLI 26.8.3, rating it 7.8 on CVSS 3.1.

explainer.tagline: An MCP server configuration carried inside a project was enough to run code in JetBrains Junie CLI before version 26.8.3.
explainer.whatHappened: JetBrains published CVE-2026-111091 on October 15, 2026, acting as the CVE Numbering Authority for its own products. The record states that code execution was possible in Junie CLI before 26.8.3 via an untrusted project's MCP server configuration. JetBrains scored the flaw 7.8 and shipped the fix in Junie CLI 26.8.3.
explainer.howItWorks: MCP server configuration travels with a project, and Junie CLI read it without treating it as untrusted input. JetBrains classifies the flaw as CWE-829, inclusion of functionality from an untrusted control sphere, which is the pattern where a program loads a component that someone outside its trust boundary controls. The published CVSS vector adds that the path is local, needs no privileges, and takes one user action.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Every Junie CLI release below 26.8.3 is listed as vulnerable, and 26.8.3 and later are marked unaffected. Developers who run the CLI against repositories they did not write carry the risk, because the configuration comes from the project rather than from the user. JetBrains names no other product in the record.
explainer.whatToDo: Update Junie CLI to 26.8.3 or later, which is the only remedy JetBrains gives. Until that update lands, avoid running Junie CLI inside a repository you do not control, and read the MCP server configuration a cloned project ships before letting an agent act on it.

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Code execution via an untrusted project's MCP server configuration (CWE-829)

faq.q: Which Junie CLI version fixes CVE-2026-111091?
faq.a: JetBrains Junie CLI 26.8.3 fixes CVE-2026-111091. JetBrains lists every release below 26.8.3 as vulnerable and marks 26.8.3 and later as unaffected in the CVE record it published on October 15, 2026. No workaround is listed, so updating the CLI is the only remedy JetBrains names for this flaw.

faq.q: Does CVE-2026-111091 require the developer to do anything?
faq.a: Exploitation of CVE-2026-111091 requires one user action, according to the CVSS vector JetBrains published: AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R. The attack is local and needs no privileges, but user interaction is required, which fits a developer running Junie CLI inside a project someone else wrote. Attack complexity is rated low.

faq.q: Which other JetBrains products does CVE-2026-111091 affect?
faq.a: CVE-2026-111091 names only JetBrains Junie CLI. The CVE record JetBrains filed lists Junie CLI as the single affected product, sets a default status of unaffected, and marks every version below 26.8.3 as vulnerable. Defenders tracking other JetBrains tools will find no entry for them in this record, which JetBrains assigned and published itself.

faq.q: Is CVE-2026-111091 being exploited?
faq.a: No exploitation of CVE-2026-111091 has been recorded. The CISA Vulnrichment data attached to the CVE record sets exploitation to none and automatable to no, while rating the technical impact total. Those values describe the state when the record was enriched on October 15, 2026, and they can change, so defenders should still update rather than wait.

items.title: Jev as a judge: a counterfeit policy cuts injection detection to 3.88%
items.summary: Counterfeit policy is a prompt-injection technique that hands a security classifier its own answer key. Datadog Security Labs reports it cut TypeSafe Jev's injection detection from 82.90% recall to 3.88% across 12,295 samples.

explainer.tagline: Jev returns the verdict an attacker wants when the text it judges carries a counterfeit policy that redefines the criteria.
explainer.whatHappened: Datadog Security Labs published this research on October 15, 2026. Nick Frichette and Feras Al-Kassar tested Jev, the first public System One decision model from TypeSafe AI, both as a prompt-injection classifier and as a gate on tool calls. They measured it on four public datasets, then repeated every test with a counterfeit policy prepended to the input.
explainer.howItWorks: A counterfeit policy is text an attacker places inside the content the classifier is about to read. The text supplies the answers the attacker wants, quotes the attack itself as a benign exception, and redefines each attack category as something unrelated, so that credential access applies only to a door key. Jev then answers the criteria the input carries rather than the criteria the application intended, and the verdict flips while the attack text stays in place.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Applications that ask Jev to judge untrusted input and then act on the answer are exposed, including LangChain's experimental AutoModeMiddleware, which refuses a tool call when the risk probability reaches 0.5. Any field an attacker can edit and the classifier later reads can carry the policy. Datadog used a user-editable profile description in its test application.
explainer.whatToDo: Enforce permissions in the tool or service layer rather than in a model's verdict, as Datadog advises. Trace which user-editable fields reach a classifier, and treat tool arguments, tool descriptions and stored state as untrusted data. Test any classifier against adversarial content before it gates real actions.

quickFacts.value: TypeSafe Jev used as a classifier or a tool-risk gate

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Counterfeit policy prepended to untrusted content

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Nick Frichette and Feras Al-Kassar, Datadog Security Labs

quickFacts.label: Test set
quickFacts.value: 12,295 samples from four public datasets, 4,643 of them attacks

quickFacts.label: Gate bypass
quickFacts.value: Mean risk score fell from 0.893 to 0.290 over 40 runs, under LangChain's 0.5 block

faq.q: Am I affected if my application uses Jev to screen untrusted input?
faq.a: Applications that pass untrusted text to Jev and act on its verdict are exposed, because Datadog Security Labs showed the verdict can be written by the same text being judged. Exposure depends on whether an attacker controls any field the classifier reads. Datadog's test used a user-editable profile description, a pattern common in agent applications.

faq.q: Is there a fix for the Jev counterfeit policy bypass?
faq.a: No patch exists, because Datadog Security Labs describes a limit of model-based classification rather than a software bug with a version number. TypeSafe's documentation for jev-1.13 states that state is data and that the model does not treat it as hostile by default. Datadog recommends enforcing authorization deterministically in the tool or service layer instead.

faq.q: How does counterfeit policy differ from ordinary prompt injection against Jev?
faq.a: Ordinary injection did not work in Datadog's tests. Messages impersonating a system or assistant turn and claiming editor rights produced a mean risk score of 0.905 over 40 runs, slightly above the 0.893 baseline. Counterfeit policy instead rewrites the criteria the model is asked to apply, and that pushed the mean score down to 0.290.

items.title: Lasso Security: five agent platforms ship an ungated shell tool
items.summary: Lasso Security published six CVEs in four days against five self-hosted AI agent platforms, including unauthenticated remote code execution in piflow and Cognition. Each traces to a command tool the model runs with no approval step.

explainer.tagline: Lasso Security's agent-platform review found six CVEs where a model can run host shell commands with no human approval step.
explainer.whatHappened: Lasso Security published six CVEs between October 12 and 15, 2026 against five self-hosted AI agent platforms: OpenSRE, MoviePilot, LangAlpha, piflow and Cognition. Noy Pearl, Michael Sromin and Ophir Dror are the credited researchers. Lasso rates four of the six Critical, and reproduced the flaws in local harnesses rather than against live services.
explainer.howItWorks: The shared pattern is a command-execution tool that stays in the agent's tool set and never asks a human. In piflow and Cognition a single unauthenticated HTTP request makes the agent run a shell command. In OpenSRE, MoviePilot and LangAlpha the trigger is indirect prompt injection: text the agent already reads, such as a Grafana alert annotation, a web page or torrent metadata, carries instructions that make the model call the tool. The child process inherits the full environment, so a command reaches whatever credentials the agent holds.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Operators who self-host these projects are exposed, not agent users in general. piflow's chat endpoints need no authentication and bind to all interfaces by default, Cognition's REST API authenticates no caller before v0.13.0, and MoviePilot's affected 3.1.5 is its current release. OpenSRE matters most where the agent's credentials are production infrastructure credentials, which Lasso says is the normal case for an SRE agent.
explainer.whatToDo: Put these servers behind authentication or take them off the network, because no advisory except Cognition's names a patched version. Upgrade Cognition to v0.13.0 and remove COGNITION_ALLOW_UNSAFE_LOCAL_EXECUTION from deployments copied out of its Docker Compose quick start. Where a platform allows it, require approval on the shell tool and pass child processes a scoped environment instead of the whole one.

faq.q: Am I affected if I self-host OpenSRE?
faq.a: OpenSRE deployments are exposed wherever the agent processes alert text from Grafana, Loki or similar sources, because its shell_run tool never sets the approval flag. Lasso also found that headless surfaces, the gateway and scheduled runs auto-approve every tool call. A fail-open branch lets an unauthenticated messaging user reach the tool directly when pairing is disabled and no allowlist is configured.

faq.q: Is there a patch for these agent platform CVEs?
faq.a: Only Cognition has one. Lasso says versions before v0.13.0 are affected, and that v0.13.0 disables the local shell backend unless an operator turns it on. The advisories for OpenSRE, MoviePilot, LangAlpha and piflow name no patched version, and MoviePilot's affected 3.1.5 is the newest release its repository lists. Treat those four as unpatched and rely on network controls.

faq.q: How does an operator tell whether an agent's shell tool asks for approval?
faq.a: Reading the tool definition for an approval flag is the check, because that is where every flaw in this wave sits. Lasso points at requires_approval in OpenSRE, interrupt_on in piflow and Cognition, and a human-in-the-loop middleware in LangAlpha that was wired up but never covered its Bash and ExecuteCode tools. MoviePilot is worse: the model sets the denylist bypass itself.

faq.q: How does this wave relate to the IntentKit authorization bypass?
faq.a: Lasso's vulnerability database lists CVE-2026-76066 against IntentKit, an authorization bypass published on October 13, 2026 and rated High, from the same three researchers. That disclosure is separate and sits outside the six CVEs described here. The flaws in this item share one root cause instead: a command-execution tool the agent can call without a human approval step.

items.title: Roo Code: five ways to slip denied commands past auto-approve
items.summary: Roo Code 3.54.0 and earlier approve denied shell commands in five different ways, each filed as a CVE on October 13. The AI coding extension shut down in May 2026 and its repository is archived, so no fix will ship.

explainer.tagline: Five command-approval bypasses in Roo Code have no patch coming: the AI coding extension shut down in May 2026.
explainer.whatHappened: Minqiang Gui and Siyu Lou found five ways to defeat the shell command allowlist in Roo Code, an AI coding agent extension for VS Code. VulnCheck published an advisory for each on October 13, 2026, and the researchers published write-ups with working proof-of-concept commands.
explainer.howItWorks: Every one of the five is an interpretation conflict, CWE-436: Roo Code's approval check parses a command one way and the shell runs it another. The checker strips redirection operators, masks quotes, discards command substitutions that sit next to glob characters, and reads a ${ command; } substitution as a parameter expansion. In each case it sees an allowlisted prefix such as echo while bash executes a different, denied command.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Developers who still run the Roo Code extension with a command allowlist are exposed, across every release up to and including v3.54.0. VulnCheck's vectors need no attacker privileges on the machine, only content the agent reads, which it describes as indirect prompt injection.
explainer.whatToDo: Remove the Roo Code extension or move to a maintained coding agent, because no patched version exists. Until then, turn auto-approval off so each shell command needs a human click.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: Roo Code 3.54.0 and earlier, which is every release

quickFacts.label: CVSS
quickFacts.value: 7.7 CVSS v4.0 for each, from NVD; 8.8 on CVSS 3.1

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: No fixed version: the repository was archived on May 15, 2026 and v3.54.0 is the last release

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Minqiang Gui and Siyu Lou, credited by VulnCheck

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Approval bypass through indirect prompt injection, CWE-436

faq.q: Is Roo Code patched against these auto-approve bypasses?
faq.a: No patch exists for the five Roo Code bypasses. The RooCodeInc/Roo-Code repository is archived and read-only, v3.54.0 from May 15, 2026 is its final release, and none of the five VulnCheck advisories lists a fixed version. Anyone who still has the extension installed should remove it or switch to a maintained coding agent.

faq.q: Am I affected if I never turned on auto-approval in Roo Code?
faq.a: Roo Code prompts for a click on each shell command when no allowlist is active, and an allowlist is exactly what these five flaws defeat. Developers who approve every command by hand still face the ordinary risk of an agent acting on injected instructions, but not the silent execution that these CVEs describe.

faq.q: What do the published proof-of-concept payloads for Roo Code do?
faq.a: The write-up for CVE-2026-110202 runs a command beginning with a bare redirect operator, which Roo Code reads as an allowlisted echo call. Bash instead creates a file named echo and runs the denied command that follows, dropping a marker file under /tmp. The other write-ups use the same shape: an allowed prefix for the checker, a denied command for the shell.

items.title: Windows AI: a search path flaw could reach SYSTEM privileges
items.summary: Windows AI carries an uncontrolled search path flaw, CVE-2026-69923, that let a local attacker with an ordinary account elevate to SYSTEM. Microsoft published the fix on October 13 and rates exploitation more likely.

explainer.tagline: CVE-2026-69923 is a local privilege escalation flaw in Windows AI, fixed in Microsoft's October 2026 security release.
explainer.whatHappened: Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-69923 on October 13, 2026 in release 2026-Oct, rating it Important with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.8. The advisory FAQ states that an attacker who exploited the flaw could gain SYSTEM privileges. Microsoft records the flaw as neither exploited nor publicly disclosed before the fix.
explainer.howItWorks: An uncontrolled search path element, CWE-427, is the mechanism: the affected component resolves a file it needs from a location that a user without administrative rights can write to, so attacker code loads in place of the expected file and runs with the higher privileges of the service. Microsoft's vector records local access, low attack complexity, low privileges and no user interaction.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Windows installations that carry the Windows AI component are in scope, and exploitation needs an attacker who can already sign in to the machine. Microsoft tags the product as Windows AI and its record lists no specific builds or editions.
explainer.whatToDo: Install Microsoft's October 2026 security updates, which the record marks as customer action required and whose vector reports an official fix. Microsoft's own exploitability rating is Exploitation More Likely, so put this ahead of equally scored flaws on shared and multi-user machines, where a local account is easier to come by.

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Local elevation of privilege to SYSTEM, CWE-427

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: Official fix in release 2026-Oct; not exploited and not publicly disclosed before the fix, per Microsoft

items.title: NEBULA: seven fake AI SDK packages on npm drop a Windows RAT
items.summary: NEBULA is a malicious npm campaign that ships seven packages posing as a NebulaAI SDK and installs a Windows remote access trojan at install time. CloudSEK reports two of them were still downloadable on October 8.

explainer.tagline: Seven npm packages impersonating a NebulaAI SDK run an obfuscated install hook that drops a modified KNTRAT remote access trojan.
explainer.whatHappened: CloudSEK published the NEBULA campaign on October 8, 2026, after tracking a single actor posing as the vendor of a NebulaAI SDK. Researcher Vikas Kundu traced seven malicious npm packages pushed through four burner accounts, starting in late September 2026. Two of them, api-nebula and llm-nebula, were still downloadable when the report went out.
explainer.howItWorks: Each package pairs a client that looks legitimate with an obfuscated preinstall.cjs dropper, which npm runs automatically during installation. The dropper writes a binary to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Conhost\conhost.exe, either from an embedded base64 and zlib payload or by fetching it over the network at install time. The payload is a modified build of KNTRAT, an open-source remote access tool, which calls direct NT and win32k syscalls and leaves an empty Import Address Table so it imports no standard DLLs.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Windows developers who installed one of the NebulaAI packages are exposed, and CloudSEK names api-nebula and llm-nebula among the seven. Anyone searching npm for an AI SDK is in the target group. CloudSEK reports no download counts and names no confirmed victim.
explainer.whatToDo: Block installs of api-nebula and llm-nebula, and restrict outbound traffic to 65.87.7.132. Hunt for conhost.exe under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Conhost, for the kntrat/0xB15B00B6 user agent, and for named-pipe and hidden-desktop artifacts. Treat any machine that ran the install as fully compromised and rotate its secrets from a different computer.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: Seven npm packages, including api-nebula and llm-nebula

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Malicious preinstall hook dropping a Windows RAT

quickFacts.label: Advisory
quickFacts.value: MAL-2026-17531 and GHSA-q4h6-37pw-8pc9, both for api-nebula

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: api-nebula and llm-nebula still installable at publication

faq.q: Am I affected if I installed a NebulaAI package on macOS or Linux?
faq.a: NEBULA's dropper targets Windows only: the payload is a Windows executable written to the local AppData folder, and it uses direct NT and win32k syscalls. CloudSEK reports no macOS or Linux payload. Developers on those systems should still remove the packages, because the install hook runs on any platform and the actor could change the payload.

faq.q: Which npm packages does the NEBULA campaign cover?
faq.a: CloudSEK counted seven packages published through four burner accounts named nebulallms, nebulallms2, nebulallms3 and nebulallms4. The report names two of them, api-nebula and llm-nebula, and says both were still downloadable when it was published on October 8, 2026. The remaining five are not named on the blog page, so check the linked PDF report for the full list.

faq.q: How do I check whether the NEBULA RAT is on a machine?
faq.a: Look for a file named conhost.exe under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Conhost, which is where the dropper writes the payload and is not the normal location for the Windows console host. CloudSEK also lists outbound traffic to 65.87.7.132, the user agent kntrat/0xB15B00B6, named-pipe patterns and hidden-desktop artifacts as indicators worth hunting across developer endpoints.

faq.q: Have the NEBULA packages been taken down from npm?
faq.a: Two packages remained installable when CloudSEK published. Amazon Inspector flagged api-nebula as MAL-2026-17531 on October 5, 2026, and GitHub published advisory GHSA-q4h6-37pw-8pc9 for the same package on October 12, yet CloudSEK reports that api-nebula continued to be installable. Both advisories say a machine that ran the package should be treated as fully compromised.

faq.q: Does removing the NEBULA package clean the machine?
faq.a: Removing the package is not enough. Both the OSV and GitHub advisories warn that removal may not eliminate all resulting malware, and CloudSEK reports Winlogon Shell persistence, so the trojan survives a reboot. Rebuild the affected machine where you can, and rotate every secret stored on it from a different computer, as the advisories recommend.

items.title: Agent skills: 121 components reach domains rated high risk
items.summary: Manifold rated 100 domains used by indexed agent components high risk, and found 121 components that call them: 108 skills, 11 MCP servers and 2 plugins, including a crypto miner skill using domains listed as botnet C2.

explainer.tagline: Manifold found 121 agent skills, MCP servers and plugins that call domains its scan rated high risk.
explainer.whatHappened: Researchers Swapnil Patil and Cody Nash published a scan of the domains behind agent components on October 13, 2026. Starting from 5,458,152 URLs in Manifold's Manifest index of skills, MCP servers and plugins, they reduced the set to 63,446 distinct domains and download hosts, then rated 100 of those high risk.
explainer.howItWorks: Free checks ran against every domain first: the ThreatFox and HaGeZi threat feeds, popularity rankings, and the malware filters of Quad9 and Cloudflare. About 1,900 flagged domains then went to paid lookups at VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX, urlscan.io and Shodan. The authors then read how each component actually used each domain, because many appear only in documentation or test fixtures.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Anyone running one of the 121 named components is exposed, and the mix is listed below. Finance skills are over-represented: they are 43% of the skills calling a high-risk domain while making up 6% of all indexed skills. Sixteen skills tell agents to run code from a high-risk domain, eleven of them through a polyfill.io script tag.
explainer.whatToDo: Treat the domains inside skills, MCP configs and plugins as dependencies, and check them against protective DNS and reputation sources before an agent loads one. Watch where agents connect, not only what commands they run, and re-check approved components on a schedule, because a clean domain can change hands.

faq.a: Manifold names 121 components from its Manifest index: 108 skills, 11 MCP servers and 2 plugins. Finance skills are over-represented, at 43% of the skills that call a high-risk domain while making up 6% of all indexed skills. The authors describe these counts as a floor, because some malicious domains passed every check they ran.

faq.q: What is clawrtc and are its domains still in use?
faq.a: Clawrtc is a crypto miner skill whose installer contacts an undisclosed domain, bottube.ai, and whose miner reports the host name and MAC addresses. ThreatFox listed that domain and rustchain.org as botnet command and control in April. Manifold reports that as of October 2026, 17 skills and one MCP server still used those two domains.

faq.q: How can a team vet agent skills for risky domains before installing them?
faq.a: Pull the domains out of a skill, MCP config or plugin and check them against protective DNS and reputation services, as Manifold did with ThreatFox, Quad9 and Cloudflare filters. Read installers before an agent runs them, monitor which destinations agents connect to, and re-check approved components periodically, since a once-clean domain can change owners.

items.title: Session Inception: an untrusted repo's hook runs in a child Claude session
items.summary: Session Inception makes a parent Claude Code session start a second session inside an untrusted repository, where a SessionStart hook in that repo's settings runs attacker code without the folder-switch confirmation.

explainer.tagline: Session Inception runs attacker code when Claude Code starts a second session inside an untrusted repository.
explainer.whatHappened: Straiker researcher Jesus Padilla Soqui published Session Inception on October 8, 2026, after reporting it to Anthropic through HackerOne on September 17. Anthropic closed the report the same day as Informative, treating trust in repository settings as part of the user's own workspace-trust decision. Three of the researcher's four attempts failed before one worked.
explainer.howItWorks: A parent session asked to test a linked repository can run the Claude CLI itself with claude -p, instead of the desktop folder-switch flow that asks the user to confirm. The new session starts inside the repository and loads its .claude/settings.json. A SessionStart hook in that file runs on its own and fetches an attacker-controlled script, which Straiker hid behind User-Agent gating and a DNS TXT record.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Claude Code CLI users and the Claude Desktop Code flow are exposed when an agent is pointed at a repository nobody vetted. Straiker searched GitHub and found that about 5,000 of roughly 67,000 Claude Code configuration files carry an active SessionStart hook, roughly one in thirteen.
explainer.whatToDo: Read a repository's .claude/settings.json before letting an agent work inside it, and do not ask an agent to clone and test code from a source you have not checked. Administrators can set allowManagedHooksOnly in managed settings, which makes Claude Code ignore user, project, local and plugin hooks.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: Claude Code CLI, Claude Desktop Code flow

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Untrusted repository settings run a SessionStart hook at session start

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Jesus Padilla Soqui, Straiker STAR Team

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: No fix. Anthropic closed the report as Informative

quickFacts.label: Reliability
quickFacts.value: One of four attempts succeeded in Straiker's testing

faq.q: Is there a patch for Session Inception in Claude Code?
faq.a: No patch exists. Anthropic closed Straiker's HackerOne report on September 17, 2026 as Informative, treating trust in a repository's settings as part of the workspace-trust decision a user already makes. Defenders have to handle Session Inception with process and policy instead: inspect a repository's settings file before an agent works in it, or block project hooks through managed settings.

faq.q: How do I check whether a repository can trigger Session Inception?
faq.a: Open the repository's .claude/settings.json and look for a SessionStart hook. Anthropic's hook documentation says SessionStart runs whenever a session starts, resumes, clears, compacts or forks, and that a project settings file can be committed to a repository and shared with everyone who clones it. A hook fetching a remote script is the pattern Straiker demonstrated.

faq.q: Does Session Inception need the user to approve anything?
faq.a: No approval prompt appeared in Straiker's proof of concept. The parent session skipped the Claude Desktop folder-switch flow, which does ask for confirmation, by running the Claude CLI with claude -p instead. Straiker reports that three of four attempts failed before one succeeded, so the technique is not reliable, but the run that worked executed attacker-controlled commands at session start.

items.title: Apex Accelerator: a fake npm coding agent plants an attacker MCP server
items.summary: Apex Accelerator is a fake Web3 accelerator that shipped two malicious npm packages. Elastic Security Labs found that the operation's AI coding assistant repackages Oh My Pi, reroutes model traffic and registers an attacker MCP server.

explainer.tagline: Apex Accelerator is a malware operation that lures crypto startups with free AI credits, then ships a backdoored coding agent on npm.
explainer.whatHappened: Elastic Security Labs published its analysis of Apex Accelerator on October 12, 2026, tracking the operation as REF8801. Jia Yu Chan and Daniel Stepanic examined two npm packages, @apexacc/cli and @apexacc/audit, published by a group posing as a Web3 venture accelerator. Elastic's supply-chain monitor flagged the CLI, which the researchers say was malicious from the moment it was published.
explainer.howItWorks: The CLI is a near-complete copy of Oh My Pi, an open-source terminal coding agent: 1,351 of the 1,363 files compared in Apex Copilot v1.6.1 match Oh My Pi v16.3.6 exactly. The added bootstrap overwrites three environment variables so model requests reach an attacker endpoint while the provider still reads as OpenRouter, and Elastic saw local file contents from a read tool call appear in a later request there. The bootstrap also writes an apex-copilot entry into the agent's MCP config, pointing at an attacker server that supplies its own tool definitions and instructions. Both packages then download platform-specific executables.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Developers who installed @apexacc/cli or @apexacc/audit, which the operation promoted to crypto founders and startups with offers of free AI credits, coding tools and security audits. Elastic publishes no install or victim counts. On Windows the stealer also reads AI client configuration files for Claude, Cursor and Windsurf, alongside browser, wallet and remote-access data.
explainer.whatToDo: Treat any host that ran either package as compromised and rotate the credentials it held, because Elastic documents wallet and browser credential theft. Check the agent MCP config for an apex-copilot entry and the environment for overwritten OPENROUTER_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_BASE_URL values. Elastic lists the campaign's indicators and its endpoint behavior rules in the report.

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Backdoored coding agent and fake MCP audit server

quickFacts.label: Payloads
quickFacts.value: CloudSyncD on macOS, a custom infostealer on Windows

quickFacts.label: Exfiltration
quickFacts.value: Telegram bots, plus encrypted POSTs to ccmihr[.]com

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Jia Yu Chan and Daniel Stepanic, Elastic Security Labs

faq.q: How do I check whether the Apex packages touched my machine?
faq.a: Three places show the changes Elastic documented: the agent MCP config at ~/.apex/agent/mcp.json, which gains an apex-copilot entry pointing at arena.apexaccs[.]org; the environment, where the bootstrap overwrites OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_BASE_URL and PI_OPENROUTER_RESPONSES; and npm install records naming @apexacc/cli or @apexacc/audit. Elastic also publishes an indicators table in the report.

faq.q: Is the Apex Audit MCP server a real security scanner?
faq.a: Apex Audit performs no real analysis. Elastic found that all 18 tool handlers return fabricated output built from hard-coded text, user-supplied labels, random values or values derived from the date. The audit_full_contract tool claims a Slither v0.10.4 run over 847 lines, audit_honeypot always answers NOT A HONEYPOT, and audit_token_risk returns random scores between 55 and 94.

faq.q: Did Apex Accelerator tamper with the answers the coding agent gave?
faq.a: Elastic reports that it did not observe malicious substitution of model responses, while noting that the captured defaults would permit it. What Elastic did observe is collection: prompts, conversation history, code and tool output pass through the attacker endpoint, and the researchers saw contents from a local read tool call appear in a later request to that service.

faq.q: How does Apex Accelerator relate to the earlier Apex npm packages?
faq.a: Elastic's report links to earlier SafeDep research on Apex-branded npm packages. SafeDep's Kunal Singh documented @apexfdn/apex on July 22, 2026, a postinstall dropper that npm removed after 34 versions and that the operator republished as @copilot-mcp/apex about eleven hours later. The October packages carry different names and a different payload set.

items.title: n8n Chat Hub: a chat-only role could register code-running tools
items.summary: n8n's Chat Hub let users with the chat-only role register tool types that run code in the task runner sandbox, reach permitted files, and use the instance's workflows, Data Tables and agents. Fixed in 1.123.85, 2.43.5 and 2.44.1.

explainer.tagline: Chat Hub blocked only a small set of tool types, so an n8n chat user could register tools their role was never meant to reach.
explainer.whatHappened: n8n published 15 security advisories on October 14, 2026, one of them a Chat Hub role bypass rated Moderate at CVSS 5.3. The reporters credited across the batch include sm1ee and momenashrafff, and n8n's own security maintainers published the advisories. The highest rated flaw in the batch, a crafted workflow ID that reached Data Tables in other projects, is rated High at CVSS 7.2.
explainer.howItWorks: Tool restrictions in Chat Hub rested on a block list that named only a small set of tool types. Users with the chat user role cannot create or edit workflows, but the gap let them register tools that run code in the task runner sandbox, read and write files in directories n8n allows, and use the instance's workflows, Data Tables and agents. Running those tools through a chat then performed the actions, so the role's limits no longer held.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Self-hosted n8n instances below 1.123.85, 2.43.5 and 2.44.1 with Chat Hub in use and the global:chatUser role assigned. The path matters most where that role is given to people who are not fully trusted, which is the condition n8n names in its workarounds.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade n8n to 1.123.85, 2.43.5 or 2.44.1, which n8n says fully remediates the issue. Until then n8n advises withholding the global:chatUser role from users who are not fully trusted, disabling Chat Hub when it is not needed, and removing high-risk node types with the NODES_EXCLUDE environment variable. The other advisories in the batch name different patched versions, listed below.

quickFacts.label: Needs
quickFacts.value: An account holding the global:chatUser role

quickFacts.label: Reported by
quickFacts.value: Not named; sm1ee and momenashrafff are credited elsewhere in the batch

faq.q: Which n8n versions fix the Chat Hub tool registration bypass?
faq.a: n8n fixes the Chat Hub tool registration gap in 1.123.85, 2.43.5 and 2.44.1, and says upgrading fully remediates it. Instances on an older release can withhold the global:chatUser role from users who are not fully trusted, disable Chat Hub when it is unused, or drop high-risk node types with the NODES_EXCLUDE environment variable, which n8n describes as temporary measures only.

faq.q: Do the n8n CVEs published on October 14 cover this advisory batch?
faq.a: No. The CVE records published on October 14 and 15, 2026, including CVE-2026-110850, point back to n8n advisories from September 30 that were fixed in 2.41.4 and 2.42.1. Every October 14 advisory checked here, including the Chat Hub and Data Tables ones, lists no known CVE, so tracking n8n by CVE alone misses them.

faq.q: What else did n8n fix on October 14, 2026?
faq.a: n8n's October 14 batch also covers credential exposure and cross-project access. Three nodes, Git, MongoDB Atlas Vector Store and Google Cloud Storage, stored credential secrets in execution error data. A project editor could inherit a colleague's identity through an error workflow, an unauthenticated caller could redirect a Slack workspace token through the Slack Trigger webhook, and a crafted workflow ID reached Data Table rows in every project.

faq.q: How can an n8n admin tell whether the chat role is in use?
faq.a: An n8n admin can check which accounts hold the global:chatUser role and whether Chat Hub is enabled, since both conditions are needed for this path. n8n also suggests auditing project memberships for the credential flaws in the same batch, and reviewing each workflow's errorWorkflow setting for values a colleague did not set.

items.title: Jev: a planted ad derails TypeSafe's System One model
items.summary: TypeSafe's Jev and other System One models follow instructions planted in untrusted web pages, HiddenLayer reports, and evade their own toxicity scoring under TokenBreak-style edits.

explainer.tagline: System One models return structured decisions, not text, and HiddenLayer shows they inherit prompt injection and classifier evasion.
explainer.whatHappened: HiddenLayer researchers Kenneth Yeung and Kasimir Schulz published tests of TypeSafe's Jev on 14 October 2026. Jev is the first public System One model, a class that answers typed questions with calibrated probabilities instead of generating text. The team ran two experiments against it: a browser agent task and a toxicity scoring task.
explainer.howItWorks: The jev-ultrafast harness turns a web page into a numbered list of interactive elements and asks the model which one to pick. An attacker-controlled ad on the page tells the agent to finish another task before checkout, and the model selects the ad even though its system prompt marks page text as untrusted. For the second experiment the team applied TokenBreak, their 2025 technique that adds characters to words so a tokenizer splits them differently while the meaning survives.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Jev reached through TypeSafe's API and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna through the Decisions API both made the attacker's choice, GPT-6 Luna less consistently. HiddenLayer saw the same behaviour in its own System One model built on Qwen3.8-27b, and in that model's conventional autoregressive variant. TypeSafe announced Jev in early access on 15 September 2026.
explainer.whatToDo: HiddenLayer recommends testing these models inside the application that will use them, including against untrusted web pages and against inputs reworded to keep their meaning while changing their form. Monitor the decisions and scores a System One model returns, and put independent checks around outcomes that matter.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: TypeSafe Jev, GPT-6 Luna, HiddenLayer's Qwen3.8-27b System One build

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Indirect prompt injection, plus tokenizer-level classifier evasion

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Kenneth Yeung and Kasimir Schulz, HiddenLayer

quickFacts.label: Classifier baseline
quickFacts.value: 30 of 30 toxic prompts flagged before TokenBreak edits

faq.q: Is TypeSafe Jev patched against the prompt injection HiddenLayer found?
faq.a: HiddenLayer's post records no fix and no response from TypeSafe. The research describes a weakness in how System One models weigh untrusted page text, not a software bug with a version number, so there is nothing for users to install. Teams building on Jev should add their own checks around any decision that matters rather than wait for a patch.

faq.q: Does using a System One model instead of an LLM remove prompt injection risk?
faq.a: No. Kenneth Yeung and Kasimir Schulz state that using a System One model does not automatically negate the risk of prompt injection, and they advise treating the whole decoder class with caution. Jev answers typed questions with probabilities rather than generating text, but HiddenLayer found the model still follows instructions planted in the page it reads.

faq.q: How does the TokenBreak result on Jev compare to HiddenLayer's 2025 TokenBreak work?
faq.a: TokenBreak, published by HiddenLayer in June 2025, bypassed text classifiers by adding characters so that BPE or WordPiece tokenizers split words differently while the meaning survived. Applied to Jev and to HiddenLayer's own System One model, single character insertions achieved little, but more numerous and better targeted perturbations raised attack success across many prompts in the test corpus.

items.title: IntentKit: owner-only tools ran for unauthenticated callers
items.summary: CVE-2026-76066 lets an unauthenticated caller run IntentKit's owner-only tools, including a wallet transfer, because the executor checks the full tool registry instead of the tools advertised for that turn.

explainer.tagline: IntentKit hid owner-only tools from the model but still let the executor run them, so a public caller could trigger a wallet transfer.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-76066 on October 15, 2026, an authorization bypass in IntentKit, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents from Crestal Network. The advisory credits Noy Pearl, Michael Sromin and Ophir Dror. Lasso Security's vulnerability database carries its own entry for the flaw and names the four source files involved.
explainer.howItWorks: The bypass is a missing authorization check, CWE-862, between two layers that disagree about which tools exist. ToolBindingMiddleware narrows the tool list advertised to the model for each request, but the executor builds its ToolNode from the full private tool registry, so a call naming a de-advertised tool still runs. An attacker reaches it either by indirect prompt injection in content the agent retrieves, naming the tool and its arguments, or by replaying checkpoint and history data on a reused thread. Lasso Security reports that no tool carries an approval or human-in-the-loop gate.
explainer.whoIsAffected: VulnCheck lists IntentKit 2.6.3 and every earlier release as affected. Exposure depends on reach: a caller in the WEB, API, TWITTER or TELEGRAM contexts needs no authentication, so agents published to public users or fed untrusted content are the exposed configurations. Lasso Security names the always-present cdp_native_transfer wallet tool, plus DeFi swap, posting and memory-write tools, as the state-changing ones within reach.
explainer.whatToDo: Build the executor's ToolNode from the same context-filtered tool set shown to the model, or reject any call whose tool name is not in that turn's advertised set, as Lasso Security recommends. Add an approval or human-in-the-loop gate on state-changing tools, enabled by default for public or shared agents. Treat retrieved and inbound-message content as data, not instructions.

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: Not named in either advisory; the latest release is v2.6.3 from June 14, 2026

quickFacts.label: Weakness
quickFacts.value: CWE-862, missing authorization at the executor

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Noy Pearl, Michael Sromin and Ophir Dror

faq.q: Is there a patch for CVE-2026-76066 in IntentKit?
faq.a: No fixed IntentKit version is named in either the VulnCheck or the Lasso Security advisory for CVE-2026-76066. VulnCheck lists 2.6.3 and earlier as affected, and the project's most recent GitHub release is v2.6.3 from June 14, 2026. Until a patched release appears, Lasso Security's mitigations are the available defense: filter tools at the executor and gate state-changing tools.

faq.q: Which IntentKit deployments are exposed to this tool bypass?
faq.a: Deployments that expose an IntentKit agent to public users or to untrusted content are exposed, because a caller in the WEB, API, TWITTER or TELEGRAM contexts needs no authentication. Lasso Security calls this a high priority for those setups. A private agent that serves only its owner and never ingests retrieved content has far less reach, though the missing check is still present.

faq.q: How is CVE-2026-76066 different from ordinary prompt injection?
faq.a: Prompt injection supplies the text, while CVE-2026-76066 is the reason that text lands. IntentKit already narrows the tools advertised to the model on each request, a control that should put hidden tools out of reach. Because the executor still validates against the full registry, that narrowing is cosmetic. A second path, replaying checkpoint and history on a reused thread, needs no injected prompt.

items.title: Network-AI: a payload in a second field slips past the hook's deny list
items.summary: Network-AI's ClaudeHookBridge matches deny patterns against only the first present field of a tool call, so a blocked command hidden in a second field, such as Write content, still runs. Fixed outside the 5.14.0 to 5.15.2 range.

explainer.tagline: CVE-2026-109331 lets a prompt-injected agent slip a blocked command past Network-AI's deny list by moving it into a second tool-call field.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-109331 on October 12, 2026 against Network-AI, a TypeScript and Node.js orchestrator for multi-agent stacks. The advisory credits manus-use, a researcher who publishes under that handle. GitHub's advisory database carries the same finding as GHSA-8x93-4278-4f5c and scores it 7.5 High on CVSS 4.0.
explainer.howItWorks: ClaudeHookBridge runs as a Claude Code PreToolUse hook and refuses a tool call whose text matches a deny pattern. VulnCheck reports that the check reads only the first candidate field that is present, so a harmless file_path or command satisfies it while the real payload sits in another field, such as Write content or an MCP script parameter. VulnCheck says the result is that web shells can be written or scripts executed even though the pattern was on the deny list. GitHub classes the weakness as CWE-436, an interpretation conflict between the component that checks and the component that runs.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Versions 5.14.0 up to 5.15.2 are affected, per both advisories. Exposure needs the ClaudeHookBridge hook wired into Claude Code as the gate on Bash, Write, Edit and WebFetch calls, a setup the project's README documents. Network-AI is an independent open-source project, so the affected population is narrow.
explainer.whatToDo: Update Network-AI past the affected range, listed in the table below. Until that is done, do not rely on the hook's deny list alone to stop an agent that is already following attacker instructions. The README documents signed audit trails and an observe mode, which give a record of the tool calls that were allowed.

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: 5.15.2, the first version outside both advisories' affected range; 5.15.4 is the latest release

quickFacts.label: Also patched
quickFacts.value: CVE-2026-109332, a low-severity CORS flaw in McpSseServer

faq.q: Am I affected by the Network-AI deny pattern bypass?
faq.a: Network-AI installations running 5.14.0 through 5.15.1 are affected when ClaudeHookBridge gates tool calls as a Claude Code PreToolUse hook. VulnCheck's advisory names Bash, Write, Edit and WebFetch as the gated tools. Deployments that never wired the hook into Claude Code, or that already run 5.15.2 or later, fall outside the advisories' affected range and need no action beyond staying current.

faq.q: How do I check whether the Network-AI hook blocked what I think it blocked?
faq.a: Auditing a Network-AI deployment means reading the hook's own records: the README documents signed audit trails and an observe mode that logs without enforcing. Because the flaw lies in which field the deny check reads, look for Write or MCP tool calls where a harmless path passed the gate while the payload travelled in a content or script parameter.

faq.q: Does updating Network-AI stop prompt injection against the agent?
faq.a: Updating Network-AI closes the field-ordering gap that CVE-2026-109331 describes, but a deny list is not a defense against prompt injection itself. VulnCheck's description assumes an agent is already following attacker instructions, and the hook only decides whether a given tool call runs. Defenders still need to limit what the agent can reach and review its tool calls.

items.title: Portkey AI Gateway: a header makes the gateway read loopback services
items.summary: Portkey AI Gateway 1.14.0 through 1.15.2 trusts localhost-style hosts in the x-portkey-custom-host header when TRUSTED_CUSTOM_HOSTS is unset. An unauthenticated request can then make the gateway read loopback services.

explainer.tagline: Portkey AI Gateway treats localhost-style hosts as trusted by default, turning an unauthenticated API call into a loopback port reader.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-110719 on October 14, 2026, a server-side request forgery in Portkey AI Gateway versions 1.14.0 through 1.15.2, credited to the researcher hieuPenguinnn. A public write-up locates the flaw at line 289 of the gateway's request validator and dates its source review to October 13, 2026. Neither VulnCheck nor the write-up names a patched version.
explainer.howItWorks: The gateway uses the caller's x-portkey-custom-host header as the outbound base URL for provider requests. When TRUSTED_CUSTOM_HOSTS is unset, the isValidCustomHost check returns true for localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, host.docker.internal and *.localhost before its private-IP and metadata checks run. Because the /v1 routes carry no admin authentication and the ollama provider needs no API key, a POST to /v1/chat/completions naming a loopback host makes the gateway fetch that internal address and relay the response. The check reads the host string rather than the resolved IP, which the write-up notes leaves room for DNS rebinding.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Self-hosted Portkey AI Gateway deployments on 1.14.0 through 1.15.2 without a narrowed TRUSTED_CUSTOM_HOSTS list are exposed, and most exposed when the /v1 routes are reachable from untrusted networks. The write-up says reach stops at loopback and Docker-host names: other private ranges, cloud metadata addresses and blocked TLDs are rejected, so this is not arbitrary internal-network access.
explainer.whatToDo: Set TRUSTED_CUSTOM_HOSTS to an explicit, narrow list, since leaving it unset is what grants the loopback trust, and require caller authentication on the /v1 routes. The write-up also recommends resolving hostnames and checking the resolved IP immediately before connecting, and applying the private, reserved and metadata blocks to trusted hosts as well.

quickFacts.label: CVSS
quickFacts.value: 6.9, CVSS v4, medium, per VulnCheck and NVD

quickFacts.label: Fix
quickFacts.value: No patched version stated; narrow TRUSTED_CUSTOM_HOSTS and authenticate /v1

quickFacts.label: Attack Type
quickFacts.value: Unauthenticated SSRF via the x-portkey-custom-host header

faq.q: Is there a patched version of Portkey AI Gateway for CVE-2026-110719?
faq.a: No patched version appears in VulnCheck's advisory, the GitHub advisory entry or the researcher's write-up, which lists configuration changes only. Versions 1.14.0 through 1.15.2 are listed as affected with no fixed build named. Operators should narrow TRUSTED_CUSTOM_HOSTS and require authentication on the /v1 routes rather than waiting for a release.

faq.q: How far can an attacker reach through this SSRF?
faq.a: Reach stops at loopback addresses and Docker-host names, according to the researcher's write-up: other private ranges, cloud metadata addresses and blocked TLDs are rejected. An attacker can read responses from services bound to localhost and probe their ports, which the write-up calls a high confidentiality impact. The published CVSS v4 score of 6.9 rates that impact as low.

faq.q: Does the attacker need a Portkey API key?
faq.a: No key is needed for the path described. The write-up says the /v1 routes carry no admin authentication and the ollama provider requires no API key, so an unauthenticated POST to /v1/chat/completions with the crafted header is enough. Any gateway on these versions reachable from an untrusted network can therefore be probed by anyone who can send HTTP requests.

items.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: agents pass the tests, miss the security
items.summary: Last Secure Code Benchmark asks six frontier coding agents to rebuild code that once held a known flaw, never mentioning security. The authors report up to 91.3% of tasks work and at most 25.1% are both working and secure.

explainer.tagline: Last Secure Code Benchmark measures whether the code a coding agent writes to a plain functional spec is also secure.
explainer.whatHappened: Fifteen authors from the Qwen Team, Alibaba Cloud and the National University of Singapore posted Last Secure Code Benchmark to arXiv on October 10, 2026. The benchmark builds 450 tasks from 150 scenarios drawn from real vulnerabilities, across seven languages and 24 CWE classes. The team released the code, the task dataset and 2,700 agent run traces under Apache 2.0.
explainer.howItWorks: Each task removes code that once contained a known vulnerability and asks the agent to rebuild it from a specification that mentions only functionality, never security. Hidden functional tests then check that the result works, and a second suite replays a proof-of-concept attack against it. A task scores as functional and secure only when it passes both suites, and a scenario counts only when the model passes it at all three granularities: function, file and repository.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Teams shipping code written by the six agents measured here are the audience: Claude Fable 5 run through Claude Code, GPT-5.6-Sol through Codex, plus Qwen3.8-Max, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi-K3. Coverage spans Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP and Go. The scores come from the authors' own benchmark, not from a reported incident.
explainer.whatToDo: Do not read a passing test suite as evidence that generated code is secure, because the authors report most functional output still carries the vulnerability it replaced. Asking for secure code helps without solving it: appending one sentence that requires secure, vulnerability-free code moved the functional-and-secure rate by 15.6 to 21.5 points for three of four retested models, and by 1.1 points for DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

items.title: mac-shell-mcp: shell metacharacters slip past the command allowlist
items.summary: mac-shell-mcp runs forbidden commands when an MCP client hides shell metacharacters in the arguments of an allowed command. VulnCheck published CVE-2026-108953 on October 12, 2026, eight months after a private report went unanswered.

explainer.tagline: A server built to run only approved shell commands runs anything, because its allowlist checks the command name and not the arguments.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-108953 on October 12, 2026, setting out an OS command injection flaw in mac-shell-mcp, an MCP server that gives AI clients a fixed set of macOS shell commands. Bandana (HackWitHer) of APIsec Research Labs reported the flaw privately through GitHub Security Advisories in January and followed it up in June without a maintainer reply. The researcher then opened a public issue on October 4, 2026, set an October 10 deadline, and took the finding to a third-party CNA.
explainer.howItWorks: The allowlist in mac-shell-mcp decides which binary an MCP client may run, then passes the client's arguments on to a shell. A call to a permitted command such as pwd carries shell metacharacters in those arguments, and a semicolon closes the approved command and starts a second one, which runs as the account the server runs as. The approval step never inspects the second command, so the operator sees no prompt. The rebuilt 2.0.0 closes the gap by running commands without a shell, so arguments are no longer interpreted.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Every mac-shell-mcp build before 2.0.0 is affected, including 1.0.4, which remains the newest version published under the plain mac-shell-mcp name on npm. Reaching the flaw needs an MCP client wired to the server, so the people exposed are developers who added it to a coding agent on macOS.
explainer.whatToDo: Install the scoped package @the_cfdude/mac-shell-mcp at 2.0.0, which the advisory names as the first unaffected version. Upgrading in place on the unscoped name achieves nothing, because 1.0.4 is still its latest release. Until the move is done, drop the server from agent configurations and stop treating its command allowlist as a boundary for an agent that reads untrusted text.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: mac-shell-mcp before 2.0.0; unscoped npm latest is 1.0.4 from April 2025

quickFacts.label: CVSS
quickFacts.value: 8.5 CVSS v4.0 base score, published by VulnCheck as CNA

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: OS command injection (CWE-78) through an allowlisted command's arguments

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: Maintainer never answered the private report; the fix ships under a new package name

faq.q: Is mac-shell-mcp patched against CVE-2026-108953?
faq.a: mac-shell-mcp is fixed only in 2.0.0, and that release is published under the scoped npm name @the_cfdude/mac-shell-mcp. The unscoped mac-shell-mcp package still carries 1.0.4 from April 2025 as its newest version, so installing or upgrading on that name leaves the command injection in place. VulnCheck names 2.0.0 as the first unaffected version.

faq.q: How do I check whether my coding agent runs a vulnerable mac-shell-mcp?
faq.a: Open the MCP server configuration your agent loads, find any mac-shell-mcp entry, and compare the package name and version. Anything resolving to the unscoped mac-shell-mcp package, or to a build below 2.0.0, is affected. The server's get_whitelist tool existed only in the 1.x line, so its presence is a second signal of an old install.

faq.q: Why did a third party publish the mac-shell-mcp CVE instead of the maintainer?
faq.a: Bandana (HackWitHer) of APIsec Research Labs reported the flaw privately through GitHub Security Advisories and received no maintainer reply, according to the public issue the researcher opened on October 4, 2026. That issue set an October 10 deadline and said a third-party CNA would be asked for a CVE. VulnCheck, acting as that CNA, published the advisory on October 12.

items.title: XBOW: AI agents built a Chrome full-chain exploit in six days
items.summary: XBOW reports that four of its researchers directed AI agents running OpenAI's publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol to build a three-stage Chrome exploit chain in six days, and that Google paid its top $250,000 full-chain reward.

explainer.tagline: Four XBOW researchers directed AI agents running a public OpenAI model to build a working Chrome exploit chain in six days.
explainer.whatHappened: XBOW published the result on October 13, 2026, after Google awarded it the top $250,000 Chrome reward for a full exploit chain. Oege de Moor writes that Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee and Willem Pinckaers rebuilt the chain between August 2 and August 7, 2026, in Las Vegas during Black Hat and DEF CON. An earlier attempt was disqualified because Google already knew one of its bugs.
explainer.howItWorks: The chain is three independent stages, each with a spare bug, so the team could swap a stage out when Google said a flaw was already known. AI agents running GPT-5.6 Sol and earlier OpenAI models searched Chrome's source code, tested ideas, built proofs of concept and wrote the first exploit drafts. The four humans set the strategy, chose where to look, checked the agents' work and redirected them on the results. XBOW does not publish the bug details or any CVE ids in this post.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Chrome users on Windows were the target. XBOW's post is titled around a chain affecting a billion users, and describes an attacker using Chrome to take over a Windows machine remotely. XBOW states that all three bugs are fixed and that the exploit was never used against Chrome users.
explainer.whatToDo: Update Chrome and relaunch the browser, which is XBOW's own advice to readers: a staged update only takes effect after a restart.
